passage:
Farmers began growing an ancient grain that had nearly disappeared. It did not produce as much as modern crops, but it survived dry weather better.
A bakery used it to make bread with a nutty taste. Customers were curious.
Agriculture students visited the farm and learned about crop diversity. Relying on only a few crops can be risky when climate or disease changes.
The ancient grain was not a magic answer. It was one more option.
Sometimes the future of food may depend on seeds from the past. Old crops can carry traits that become valuable again under new conditions.
